description.en:
Ontology capturing the legal landscape governing AI-driven automated
        decision-making in medical contexts. Covers CJEU precedents on GDPR
        Art.22, UPC/EPO patent litigation in MedTech, the EU AI Act high-risk
        regime, MDR 2017/745, PLD 2024/2853, EHDS 2025/327, DGA 2022/868,
        and Data Act 2023/2854 — with full precedent chains, SHACL runtime
        constraints, and compliance obligation mappings.
        Imports: W3C DPV v2.0 (data privacy vocabulary), AIRO (AI risk ontology),
        ELI (European Legislation Identifier), ECLI (European Case Law Identifier).
description.undefined: OWL ontology mapping EU regulatory frameworks (GDPR, AI Act, MDR, PLD, EHDS, DGA, Data Act) to medical AI automated decision-making, CJEU case law, UPC patent litigation, and compliance obligations.

comment.en: TSD Art.2 protects model weights, training data schemas, and architecture as trade secrets. AI Act Art.13 requires deployers to receive sufficient information about high-risk AI system capabilities and limitations. C-203/22 §§60-70 sets the mandatory floor: controller cannot invoke TSD Art.2 to deny all causal explanation of an automated decision — disputed information must be produced to the competent supervisory authority or court for balance. AI Act Art.78 ensures national authority confidentiality but does not disapply Art.13 disclosure to deployers. TSD Art.5 is the only legislative bridge but its scope in the medical AI context remains unresolved pending a CJEU reference on Art.22 and clinical AI.

labels.en: TSD Art.2 Trade Secret vs. AI Act Art.13 + GDPR Art.15(1)(h) — Core Transparency Tension

comment.en: C-203/22 Dun & Bradstreet §§60-70 limits trade-secret defence: a controller cannot refuse all causal explanation on trade-secret grounds. The precise boundary between permitted limitation and impermissible derogation is determined case-by-case.

labels.en: Data Act Art.15 trade secret vs. AI Act Art.13 + GDPR Art.15(1)(h) transparency

comment.en: Two separate conformity assessment pathways for the same SaMD. MDCG AIB 2025-1 provides a procedural joint-assessment mechanism but does not harmonise the substantive requirement sets.

labels.en: MDR Annex IX conformity vs. AI Act Art.43 conformity assessment

comment.en: EHDS Art.35 grants patients an unconditional right to opt out of secondary health data use. Where opt-out rates are elevated in a clinically significant subpopulation, the resulting training dataset violates AI Act Art.10(3) representativeness. No legislative safe harbour bridges these positions.

labels.en: EHDS Art.35 opt-out vs. AI Act Art.10(3) representativeness

comment.en: PLD Art.11 defect presumption applies where it is excessively difficult for the claimant to prove defect. AI Act Art.9-compliant risk management documentation may rebut the presumption but no legislative safe harbour confirms this.

labels.en: PLD Art.10 defect presumption vs. AI Act Art.9 risk management

comment.en:
PLD Art.4 imposes strict liability; AI Act conformity assessment is not a
        defence to PLD claims. A CE-marked AI-SaMD that passes AI Act conformity
        assessment may still be 'defective' under PLD if it fails in real-world
        deployment. The two regimes do not create a safety harbour from each other.

labels.en: PLD Strict Liability vs. AI Act Conformity Defence

comment.en:
EPC Art.83 requires public disclosure of training data structure to maintain patent validity.
        GDPR Art.15(1)(h) + C-203/22 require actionable explanations to data subjects.
        The EPO disclosure may inadvertently establish a baseline that strengthens GDPR access rights,
        eroding TSD Art.2 trade secret shields that might otherwise limit GDPR Art.15 responses.
        TSD Art.9 judicial confidentiality measures do not apply to EPO prosecution, leaving no
        mechanism to contain the disclosure baseline once it enters the public patent record.

labels.en: EPC Art.83 Sufficiency Disclosure vs. GDPR Art.15(1)(h) + TSD Art.2 Secrecy

comment.en:
Deep-learning medical AI is inherently opaque (black-box). Patent protection incentivises
        secrecy over model weights. EU AI Act Art.13 and C-817/19 black-box prohibition
        require transparency for high-risk AI systems, creating structural tension with
        commercial IP protection strategies. TSD Art.2 reinforces the secrecy interest;
        TSD Art.5 carve-outs are the only legislative bridge, but their scope is unresolved.

labels.en: Black-Box Patent Protection vs. EU AI Act Transparency Obligation

comment.en: DGA Art.10 prohibits data-sharing intermediaries from using shared data for purposes beyond the sharing service. Integrated AI development models in which intermediary and developer are related entities require structural business model restructuring that no guidance resolves.

labels.en: DGA Art.10 neutrality obligation vs. AI Act Art.10 data governance

comment.en: EPO patent prosecution optimises for broad technical-effect claims (wider scope = stronger IP protection); MDR Annex II requires precise intended-purpose specification (narrower scope = easier clinical evaluation); AI Act Art.9/13 requires intermediate characterisation covering intended purpose plus reasonably foreseeable misuse. The same SaMD must be described at opposing granularity levels across three institutional knowledge spaces. No EPO, MDCG, or AI Office guidance addresses this triangular scope alignment problem.

labels.en: EPO G-II §3.3 broad claim scope vs. MDR Annex II §1.1 + AI Act Art.9/13 intended purpose

comment.en: Data Act. Applies from 2025-09-12. Governs data sharing obligations for IoT-generated data (medical devices, wearables) and B2G/B2B data access for AI development.

General Data Protection Regulation. Core data protection framework; Art.22 governs solely automated decision-making, Art.15/15(1)(h) the right of access and meaningful information, Art.9 special category health data, Art.35 DPIA obligation.
Data Governance Act. Applies from 2023-09-24. Creates data intermediaries, data altruism organisations, and re-use frameworks for public sector health data.
European Health Data Space. Governs primary use (MyHealthData) and secondary use of health data for research, innovation, and AI training. In force 2025-03-26.

Agreement on a Unified Patent Court (in force 2023-06-01). Establishes the UPC as a supranational court for infringement and revocation of European patents across contracting states. Key for medtech AI: opt-out strategy, PI threshold ('more likely than not' invalidity standard from 10x v. NanoString CoA), EPO-UPC divergence risk.
Revised Product Liability Directive. AILD was withdrawn 2025-02-10; PLD 2024 is the operative EU strict-liability instrument for AI systems as 'products'.

European Patent Convention (in force 1977-10-07). Governs patentability of AI/medical-AI inventions (Art.52 exclusions), sufficiency of disclosure for ML models (Art.83), and EPO opposition/appeal proceedings. Administered by EPO; distinct from EU law but intersects via UPC.

EU Trade Secrets Directive. Harmonises civil-law protection of undisclosed know-how and business information. Key for medical AI: model weights, training data schemas, and proprietary algorithms qualify as trade secrets under the Art.2 three-part test. Art.5 carve-outs limit the secrecy shield when exercise of the right to information is at stake — directly engaged by GDPR Art.15(1)(h) and AI Act Art.13 transparency obligations.

comment.en: The prohibition in Art.22 cannot be circumvented by splitting the automated decision across multiple actors (scoring agency + final decision maker). Both may bear responsibility.

'Solely' is assessed functionally: formal human intervention that does not constitute substantive review (rubber-stamping) does not negate the 'solely' requirement. The decisive weight given to the automated output is the test.
Art.15(1)(h) requires actionable explanations in non-technical language, identifying which inputs affected the output and the main reasoning path. Abstract mathematical formulas are insufficient.
A 'decision' under Art.22 encompasses any act producing legal or similarly significant effects. Automated scoring creating probabilities relied upon by third parties constitutes a 'decision'.
Art.22(1) is a prohibition rule, not merely a right to object. Exceptions in Art.22(2) are exhaustive; safeguards in Art.22(3) are mandatory when an exception applies.
Non-transparent, self-learning ML risk assessment systems may not be used for decisions with significant impact. Pre-determined criteria and regular review are required.
Patients have an unconditional right to a complete copy of their medical records, free of charge, including all AI-generated diagnostic outputs, in a faithful and comprehensible format.
Any positive match from automated PNR analysis must be subject to individual non-automated review before any measure is taken. Establishes constitutional minimum for meaningful human intervention.
Data subjects must be informed of data transfers; establishes foundational transparency obligation.
Automated assessment criteria must not be based on health status. AI systems trained on medical history data may not use health condition as a discriminatory classification basis.
Large-scale automated processing must satisfy: (a) targeted scope, (b) purpose limitation, (c) temporal limitation. Failure at any level invalidates the entire processing system.

comment.en: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA).

Three-part cumulative test: information must be (1) secret (not generally known or readily accessible), (2) have commercial value because it is secret, and (3) be subject to reasonable steps to keep it secret. All three must hold for ML model weights or training data to qualify.

labels.en: TSD Article 2 — Definition of Trade Secret

comment.en: High-risk AI providers must establish and maintain a risk management system throughout the AI system lifecycle. Iterative process; complements MDR post-market surveillance.

labels.en: AI Act Art.9 — Risk Management System

Trade secret protection does not apply where disclosure is required for the exercise of the right to information. Directly engaged when a data subject invokes GDPR Art.15(1)(h) or AI Act Art.86 for an explanation of an automated medical decision — controller cannot use TSD Art.2 to block all causal explanation (C-203/22 §§60-70).
Data holders must share IoT-generated health data with third parties at user request. Creates AI training data supply chain implications for medical device manufacturers.

comment.en: Rebuttable presumption of defect where: defendant fails to disclose; product does not comply with mandatory safety requirements; obvious malfunction occurs. Reduces claimant's evidential burden.

In public health emergencies, governments may require medical AI companies to share health data. Applies to epidemic surveillance AI and clinical trial datasets.

comment.en: Prohibition on solely automated individual decision-making.

comment.en: Enhanced protection for special category data (including health data) in automated decisions.
Safeguards when exceptions apply: human intervention, right to express views, contest decision.
Notification requirements for data intermediaries facilitating health data exchange between data subjects and AI developers. Must be neutral — cannot use data for own purposes.
Exceptions: contract necessity, explicit consent, EU/Member State law.
Data sharing obligation is limited by trade secret protection — manufacturers may refuse where disclosure would reveal protected business information. Key tension with AI transparency obligations.

comment.en: Core prohibition: individuals shall not be subject to solely automated decisions producing significant effects.

Deployers (e.g., hospitals using third-party AI) must ensure human oversight, monitor performance, inform affected persons, maintain logs. Creates shared responsibility with providers.
Expressly includes software (including AI systems) in the definition of 'product'. SaMD under MDR may simultaneously be a 'product' under PLD.

comment.en: Data Act. Applies from 2025-09-12. Governs data sharing obligations for IoT-generated data (medical devices, wearables) and B2G/B2B data access for AI development.

General Data Protection Regulation. Core data protection framework; Art.22 governs solely automated decision-making, Art.15/15(1)(h) the right of access and meaningful information, Art.9 special category health data, Art.35 DPIA obligation.
Data Governance Act. Applies from 2023-09-24. Creates data intermediaries, data altruism organisations, and re-use frameworks for public sector health data.
European Health Data Space. Governs primary use (MyHealthData) and secondary use of health data for research, innovation, and AI training. In force 2025-03-26.
